title: Corponation Zone Law: Sovereignty Within the City
body:
Corponation Zones — officially designated Autonomous Corporate Jurisdictions, or ACJs — are geographically bounded areas within Meridian 88 where a single corponation exercises primary legislative and enforcement authority. As of 2199, there are 23 active ACJs in the megacity, ranging from the 4-block Helios Biopharma Research Enclave in Evanston to the 14-square-kilometer Ringo CorpoNation Industrial Campus that occupies most of what was formerly Gary, Indiana. Within an ACJ, the corponation's internal code — typically called a Charter of Operations — supersedes Meridian municipal law on most civil and commercial matters, with narrow carve-outs for certain federal statutes that the courts have largely stopped enforcing.

Entry into an ACJ constitutes legal consent under the Meridian Zone Access Protocol of 2167. A person passing through a designated entry checkpoint — marked by the standardized yellow-and-black threshold pylons — is automatically bound by the host corponation's Charter of Operations for the duration of their visit. This includes consent to biometric scanning, behavioral monitoring, and in some Charters, mandatory arbitration for any dispute arising within the zone. The Ringo Charter, for example, requires that all disputes involving zone personnel be resolved through Ringo's internal Conflict Resolution Bureau, with no right of external appeal except for capital offenses — and even the definition of 'capital offense' is left to Ringo's own legal code.

Criminal law within ACJs operates on a dual-track system. Offenses committed by non-employees are handled through Meridian's Civic Court system, but only after the ACJ's own security apparatus has completed a preliminary investigation — a process that can take up to 72 hours, during which the individual may be held in the corponation's own detention facilities. Offenses committed by employees are handled entirely internally unless the employee explicitly waives internal jurisdiction, which almost no employment contract permits. The Lakeview Human Rights Collective has documented 34 cases since 2195 in which individuals died in ACJ detention facilities without any external investigation being conducted.

The legal relationship between ACJs and the Meridian civic government is managed through a body called the Jurisdictional Coordination Council, which meets quarterly in the Millennium Civic Center and has no enforcement powers. Its primary function is to maintain the official map of ACJ boundaries, which is updated irregularly and is often 6-18 months out of date. This matters because ACJ boundaries expand through a process called 'Zone Extension Filing,' which requires only 30 days' notice and a filing fee — leading to a practice critics call 'zone creep,' in which ACJs incrementally absorb adjacent municipal areas. The Rogers Park neighborhood association has filed 11 formal protests against Axiom Data Systems' ongoing zone extensions since 2197; none have resulted in boundary rollbacks.
